results.title: CycleGAN Architecture | davidiommi/3D-CycleGan-Pytorch-MedImaging ...
results.content: ### Core Components The architecture consists of four primary networks: * `netG_A`: Transforms images from domain A to domain B (e.g., MRI → CT) * `netG_B`: Transforms images from domain B to domain A (e.g., CT → MRI) * `netD_A`: Distinguishes between real domain B images and fake domain B images (generated by `netG_A`) * `netD_B`: Distinguishes between real domain A images and fake domain A images (generated by `netG_B`) Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 85-97 ### CycleGAN Architecture Diagram Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 121-126 The core innovation of CycleGAN is its cycle consistency mechanism, which ensures that translating an image to another domain and back should yield the original image, enforcing the preservation of structure and content. **GAN Loss for Generators**: * `loss_G_A`: Encourage `netG_A` to generate images that `netD_A` classifies as real B * `loss_G_B`: Encourage `netG_B` to generate images that `netD_B` classifies as real A * `loss_cycle_A`: L1 loss between `rec_A` and `real_A`, weighted by `lambda_A` * `loss_cycle_B`: L1 loss between `rec_B` and `real_B`, weighted by `lambda_B` * `loss_idt_A`: L1 loss between `netG_A(real_B)` and `real_B`, encourages generator to preserve identity when input is already from the target domain * `loss_idt_B`: L1 loss between `netG_B(real_A)` and `real_A`, similar to above * `loss_cor_coe_GA`: Correlation between `fake_B` and `real_A`, weighted by `lambda_co_A` * `loss_cor_coe_GB`: Correlation between `fake_A` and `real_B`, weighted by `lambda_co_B` * Helps maintain structural similarities between source and generated images Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 171-189 ### Discriminator Losses * `loss_D_A`: Binary classification loss for real B vs fake B (from image pool) * `loss_D_B`: Binary classification loss for real A vs fake A (from image pool) Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 128-147 To stabilize training, an image pool is used to store previously generated images: Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 8-35 The optimization process alternates between updating generators and discriminators: The optimization process in detail: 1. **Forward Pass**: Generate fake images and reconstructions * Calculate generator losses (GAN, cycle, identity, correlation) * Backpropagate and update generator weights * Calculate discriminator losses for both domains * Backpropagate and update discriminator weights Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 196-209 Key parameters that affect the CycleGAN architecture: Sources: models/cycle_gan_model.py 42-61 Integration with 3D Medical Imaging This implementation specifically adapts CycleGAN for 3D medical images: 1.

Abstract: Domain adaptation is of huge interest as labeling is an expensive and error-prone task, especially on pixel-level like for semantic segmentation. Based on a training set (X,y) with X ⊂S, we train a neural network f in a su-pervised manner on the synthetic domain solving the desired task (e.g., semantic segmentation or classifi-cation). results.title: Introduction to CycleGAN. In this article, we discuss the… | by Abdulkader Helwan | Medium
results.content: ## Introduction In this series of articles, we’ll present a Mobile Image-to-Image Translation system based on a Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks (CycleGAN). We’ll build a CycleGAN that can perform unpaired image-to-image translation, as well as show you some entertaining yet academically deep examples. ## CycleGAN Model A CycleGAN model enables training a deep convolutional neural network (deep CNN) to perform image-to-image translations by mapping input and output images from unpaired datasets. The network learns how to map an input image to an output image using a training set of images. The typical CycleGAN architecture includes two generators and two discriminators that work in sync to map images from the source domain to the target domain and vice versa using the same model. GAB generates images for the first domain (Domain A). In other words, it transforms images from Domain A to Domain B — from horses to zebras. Each generator has a corresponding discriminator that detects whether the generated image is real or fake. So we have two mapping functions — G and F: A represents images from Domain A, and B represents the desired output images from Domain B. ## CycleGAN Generator A CycleGAN generator is an autoencoder that takes an input image, extracts features from it, and generates another image. The generator network consists of three main stages: The encoder stage includes three 2D convolutional layers followed by an instance normalization layer and an activation function (ReLU). The latter maps input from a 256 by 256 image to a single scalar output, which represents “real” or “fake.” The CycleGAN discriminator maps from the 256 by 256 image to an N by N array of outputs X. However, in CycleGAN, adversarial loss is applied to both generators that are trying to generate images of their corresponding domains. A generator aims to minimize the loss against its discriminator in order to finally generate real images. CycleGAN uses two cycle-consistency losses to regularize the mappings: These two are calculated in order to make sure that if an image is translated from one domain to another (A to B) and then back (B to A), the same results will be obtained.

results.title: [1711.03213] CyCADA: Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Domain Adaptation
results.content:
Title: [1711.03213] CyCADA: Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Generative pixel-level domain adaptation models perform similar distribution alignment—not in feature space but rather in raw pixel space—translating source data to the “style” of a target domain. We propose Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Domain Adaptation (CyCADA), which adapts representations at both the pixel-level and feature-level while enforcing local and global structural consistency through pixel cycle-consistency and semantic losses. CyCADA unifies prior feature-level (Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015; Tzeng et al., 2017) and image-level (Liu & Tuzel, 2016b; Bousmalis et al., 2017b; Shrivastava et al., 2017) adversarial domain adaptation methods together with cycle-consistent image-to-image translation techniques (Zhu et al., 2017), as illustrated in Table 1. Table 1: Our model, CyCADA, may use pixel, feature, and semantic information during adaptation while learning an invertible mapping through cycle consistency. The Domain Transfer Network (Taigman et al., 2017b) trains a generator to transform a source image into a target image by enforcing consistency in the embedding space. We find that in the case of the small domain shifts between USPS and MNIST, the pixel space adaptation by which we train a classifier using images translated using CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017), performs very well, outperforming or comparable to prior adaptation approaches. The task is to assign a semantic label to each pixel in the input image, e.g. We limit our evaluation to the unsupervised adaptation setting, where labels are only available in the source domain, but we are evaluated solely on our performance in the target domain. First, we perform image-space adaptation and map our source data into the target domain. Next, we perform pixel-level adaptation using our image space GAN losses together with semantic consistency and cycle consistency losses. For cycle-consistent image level adaptation, we followed the network architecture and hyperparameters of CycleGAN(Zhu et al., 2017). When or (Figure 9 for Semantic Segmentation ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ CyCADA: Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Domain Adaptation") left), the results lack any consistent semantics making it difficult to perceive the style of the transformed image.
